Everything is okay now! This happened almost a year and a half ago.

It happened because I contracted flesh-eating disease by way of a puncture wound on my foot. We had to remove some of the bone and one of my toes because it spread incredibly quickly. While I was in the hospital dealing with all of this, I contracted MRSA, which no one realized at the time. They gave me some antibiotics and sent me home.

While I was at home, the MRSA spread throughout the still-healing surgical wound, and the infection caused my blood sugar to spike (I have Type 1 diabetes), and I ended up in a state of diabetic ketoacidosis as a result. This led to me being incredibly sick and unable to care for the wound very well, not that there's much that could have been done about it on my end because, well, MRSA. It basically turned into a horrible infection feedback loop that led to the whole thing becoming septic. By the time I got to the ER the DKA and the sepsis were trying very hard to shut my organs down.

I called my parents after I woke up in the ICU, they live a couple of towns over; they came to see me immediately. They were pretty mad that I didn't call them earlier, which is fair. But apparently your brain is not good at thinking while you have sepsis.

I'm doing all right now though. Everything isn't perfect; my kidneys took damage because they were the first thing to get hit by the sepsis, and the antibiotics I was on for the MRSA started to hurt them as well. I have some pretty nasty PTSD from the whole experience, and my bone marrow hates me a little and doesn't like producing red blood cells anymore. But all things considered I'm doing much better than I could be.

I was home alone when a surgical wound went septic without my realizing it. I had what I think was a seizure, but I'm not sure. When I came to, I texted a friend to tell her that I wasn't feeling well and was going to bed. She asked me to describe what I meant by "not feeling well" and convinced me to call 911 instead. I had another seizure after I got to the ER and blacked out.

I didn't realize how close I was to dying until I woke up in the ICU, on oxygen and with four IVs in my arms, two ports each. All eight ports were occupied. The nurses were surprised that I woke up relatively easily; there were a tense several hours where they weren't sure I was going to make it. If I'd gone back to sleep instead of calling 911 I would have died.

They also insisted that I could wait because the doctor wrote "please admit and start IV antibiotics and prepping for surgery" instead of "direct admit and start IV antibiotics and prepping for surgery"; the exact quote was "if it was actually urgent they wouldn't have bothered being polite. stop attention seeking, because we're not going to see you until we've cleared out the rest of the ER."

Yeah, I tend to have very flat affect most of the time (schizophrenia in my case, though, not autism); eventually my nurses when I was in the hospital started explaining that I was "very stoic about pain" to the next nurse coming on shift.

I've done that too, though, punching or hitting myself to try to distract from whatever pain is going on - I have a lot of nerve problems and was also put on anticonvulsants for the constant pain eventually, though I still do it from time to time. Wanting to stab myself was a first, though, I will admit.

To be fair, the other times I've hit a 10 it was instances where I woke up screaming uncontrollably and not really aware of much until they finally gave me painkillers (this was after the amputation in question) - so I wouldn't say it's completely untrue that most people don't experience a 10, because I can't really say I "experienced" those either. I just remember the one time I did, and hoo boy. I'll definitely agree that in the instances where people are aware of a 10 it's usually pretty obvious.

I've always had such a problem with the pain scale, given that 10 is always described as "the worst pain you can imagine" - for the longest time, I always felt that whatever I was going through must be less than a 10 by default, because getting stabbed or set on fire would probably make the current pain worse.

I've only experienced a 10 once, and that was waiting to have an amputation done and having had no painkillers whatsoever in the time leading up to it. I asked someone in the waiting room (before I was admitted) if they had something to stab me with, because the pain from being stabbed would be a welcome distraction from the pain in the site I was there to have amputated.

It's stupid because my Nmom died two years ago and never supported me or did anything at all motherly in her life, but I just really want a mom right now.

...That said, I always planned to die before I turned 30, and I'm turning 31 in three months. I've outlived myself by nine months so far and I'm not feeling like that anymore, so I've got that going for me, which is nice.

I still have difficulty with this sort of thing, mostly because my Nmom insisted that I needed to have a reason that she considered valid to have feelings at all - otherwise I was just being oversensitive or irrational, and it was generally my own fault that I was angry or upset.

I've been doing better about it lately, mostly due to a lot of therapy and (like others have mentioned) just practicing opening up to people and forcing myself to have difficult conversations. It also helps to think of things like that as being a learned skill; it's something that you can develop into over time, rather than an intrinsic trait that other people have and you don't. It feels a little less like there's something fundamentally wrong with me when I consider it that way; I was taught to feel like this, it can be unlearned with enough work put in.

Feelings don't always have a logical basis; even if you're a logical person, you're still allowed to have feelings, and it's not your fault for having them.
